---
title: "Media, Design, and Cultural Expression（媒体、设计与文化表达）"
---

## Media, Audience, and Attention（媒体、受众与注意力）

Media（媒体）are the channels, platforms, and institutions through which information（信息）, entertainment（娱乐）, ideas（思想）, and cultural content（文化内容）are produced, distributed, and consumed by audiences. Traditional media（传统媒体）include newspapers（报纸）, magazines（杂志）, radio（广播）, television（电视）, books（书籍）, and film（电影）. Digital media（数字媒体）include websites（网站）, social media platforms（社交媒体平台）, streaming services（流媒体服务）, podcasts（播客）, blogs（博客）, and online news outlets（在线新闻媒体）. Media shape how people understand the world by selecting what information to present（选择呈现什么信息）, how to present it（如何呈现）, and what to omit（省略什么）— a process called agenda-setting（议程设置）that determines which issues receive public attention and which remain invisible.

An audience（受众）is the group of people who receive, interpret, and respond to media content. Audiences are not passive recipients（被动接受者）of media messages; they actively select（主动选择）, interpret（解释）, evaluate（评价）, and respond to content based on their prior knowledge（先前知识）, beliefs（信念）, values（价值观）, social position（社会位置）, and personal experience（个人经验）. Different audience members may understand the same media message differently — a news report about immigration policy（移民政策）may be interpreted as informative（信息性的）by one viewer, as biased（有偏见的）by another, and as irrelevant（无关的）by a third, depending on their political orientation（政治取向）, personal experience with immigration, and trust in the media source（对媒体来源的信任）.

Attention（注意力）is the most valuable and scarce resource（最有价值且稀缺的资源）in the contemporary media environment. With an effectively unlimited supply of content — millions of articles, videos, posts, and podcasts produced daily — media organisations and platforms compete intensely（激烈竞争）for a finite amount of human attention. The design of digital media platforms — algorithms（算法）, notifications（通知）, autoplay（自动播放）, infinite scroll（无限滚动）, personalised recommendations（个性化推荐）— is optimised to capture and hold attention（捕获并保持注意力）for as long as possible, because attention generates advertising revenue（广告收入）, user data（用户数据）, and platform engagement（平台参与度）.

The attention economy（注意力经济）treats human attention as a scarce commodity（稀缺商品）that is bought, sold, and competed for. Platforms that capture more attention can sell more advertising, collect more data, and generate more revenue. This economic structure（经济结构）creates incentives to produce content that is engaging（引人入胜的）, sensational（耸人听闻的）, emotionally provocative（情感挑衅性的）, or polarising（极化的）— because such content generates more clicks（点击）, shares（分享）, comments（评论）, and time spent on the platform — which may not be the same as content that is accurate（准确的）, balanced（平衡的）, nuanced（细致的）, or genuinely informative（真正有信息量的）. The attention economy therefore shapes not only what content is produced but also how it is presented, with implications for the quality of public discourse（公共话语质量）, democratic deliberation（民主审议）, and individual wellbeing（个人福祉）.

Media, audience, and attention therefore represent the mechanism through which information, entertainment, and ideas are produced, distributed, and consumed and how the competition for attention shapes what content is produced and how it is presented. The vocabulary of media — media, audience, attention, attention economy, agenda-setting, platform engagement — names the channels through which content reaches audiences and the economic forces that determine what content is produced and promoted. Media texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from content production through audience attention to the social outcomes that determine whether media informs public discourse or polarises it.

## Information Flow and Public Opinion（信息流动与公众意见）

Information flow（信息流动）refers to how information moves through society — who produces it, who distributes it, who receives it, how quickly it spreads, and how it is transformed along the way. In the pre-digital era（前数字时代）, information flow was largely one-directional（单向的）and controlled by a small number of institutions — newspapers, television networks（电视网络）, radio stations（广播电台）, and publishing houses（出版社）— that acted as gatekeepers（把关人）, deciding what information reached the public. Today, information flows through many channels simultaneously（同时通过多个渠道流动）, and anyone with internet access can create and share content, dramatically increasing the volume（数量）, speed（速度）, and diversity（多样性）of information available while also making it more difficult to distinguish reliable sources（可靠来源）from unreliable ones（不可靠来源）.

The speed of information flow has increased dramatically. News that once took days or weeks to spread through print media（印刷媒体）can now reach millions of people within minutes through social media and online news. Important information — public health alerts（公共健康警报）, emergency notifications（紧急通知）, scientific findings（科学发现）— can be shared quickly and widely. Misinformation（虚假信息）and disinformation（蓄意虚假信息）can spread just as fast, sometimes faster than accurate information because sensational or emotionally charged content（情感化内容）generates more engagement and sharing.

Public opinion（公众意见 / 舆论）is the collective view（集体观点）of the public on particular issues, events, or policies. Public opinion is shaped by personal experience, family and social networks（家庭和社会网络）, education, and — increasingly — media exposure（媒体接触）. Media play a particularly important role because they provide much of the information people use to form opinions about issues they do not experience directly — foreign affairs（外交事务）, economic policy（经济政策）, scientific research（科学研究）, environmental issues（环境问题）. Most people do not personally observe climate change, evaluate economic data, or assess medical evidence; they rely on media to provide the information that forms the basis of their opinions.

Media influence public opinion through several mechanisms. Agenda-setting（议程设置）determines which issues receive coverage（获得报道）and therefore which issues the public considers important. Framing（框架设定）determines how issues are presented — what aspects are emphasised（强调什么方面）, what language is used（使用什么语言）, what context is provided（提供什么语境）— shaping how audiences interpret events. Priming（启动效应）makes certain considerations（特定考量）more accessible in people's minds, influencing what criteria they use to evaluate political leaders or policy proposals. Public opinion can also influence media, as media organisations respond to what their audiences are interested in, creating a reciprocal relationship（相互关系）between media coverage and public concern.

The rise of social media has fundamentally changed how public opinion forms and evolves. People encounter information from many sources simultaneously — professional journalists（专业记者）, friends and family, influencers（意见领袖）, algorithms, and anonymous accounts（匿名账户）. This fragmented media environment（碎片化媒体环境）can lead to echo chambers（信息茧房 / 回音室）where people are exposed primarily to information and opinions that confirm their existing beliefs, reinforcing polarisation（强化极化）and making it more difficult for societies to develop shared understanding（共同理解）of facts and issues.

Information flow and public opinion therefore represent the mechanism through which information moves through society and how that movement shapes the collective views of the public. The vocabulary of information flow — information flow, gatekeeper, public opinion, agenda-setting, framing, priming, echo chamber — names the processes through which information reaches the public and the mechanisms through which media influence what people think about and how they interpret events. Media texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from information production through media distribution to the public opinion outcomes that determine whether societies develop shared understanding of facts and issues or whether fragmented media environments reinforce polarisation and make democratic deliberation more difficult.

## Digital Platforms and Algorithms（数字平台与算法）

Digital platforms（数字平台）are online systems that connect users, content, services, and advertisers（广告商）, facilitating interactions（促进互动）and transactions（交易）at massive scale. Social media platforms（社交媒体平台）— Facebook, Instagram, X (formerly Twitter), TikTok（抖音国际版）— connect people and allow them to create, share, and consume content. Video platforms（视频平台）— YouTube, Netflix（网飞）— connect content creators with viewers. E-commerce platforms（电子商务平台）— Amazon（亚马逊）, Alibaba（阿里巴巴）— connect buyers and sellers. Search engines（搜索引擎）— Google（谷歌）, Bing — connect users with information. These platforms have become the primary infrastructure（主要基础设施）through which billions of people access information, communicate, shop, and participate in public life.

Algorithms（算法）are sets of computational rules（计算规则）that platforms use to sort（排序）, filter（过滤）, rank（排名）, and recommend（推荐）content to users. On social media, algorithms determine which posts appear in a user's feed（信息流）, in what order, and with what prominence（显著度）. On video platforms, algorithms recommend what to watch next（接下来观看什么）based on viewing history（观看历史）and the behaviour of similar users. On search engines, algorithms rank web pages（网页排名）by estimated relevance（估计的相关性）to the user's query（查询）. These algorithmic decisions（算法决策）are made automatically, at scale, and in real time（实时）, processing billions of pieces of content for billions of users every day.

Algorithms are designed to achieve specific objectives（特定目标）defined by the platforms that create them — typically maximising user engagement（最大化用户参与度）, increasing time spent on the platform（增加平台停留时间）, or generating advertising revenue（产生广告收入）. These objectives shape what content is promoted（推广什么内容）and what is suppressed（压制什么内容）. Content that generates strong emotional reactions（引发强烈情感反应的内容）— outrage（愤怒）, fear（恐惧）, excitement（兴奋）, amusement（娱乐）— tends to produce more engagement and is therefore promoted by engagement-optimising algorithms. Content that is complex（复杂的）, nuanced（细致的）, or requires sustained attention（需要持续关注）may generate less engagement and receive less algorithmic promotion.

Algorithmic curation（算法策展）— the use of algorithms to select and organise what content users see — raises important questions about transparency（透明度）, accountability（问责）, and democratic values（民主价值观）. What values should guide algorithmic decisions? Should platforms be responsible for the content their algorithms promote? How can users understand and control what algorithms show them? The opacity（不透明性）of proprietary algorithms（专有算法）— which platforms typically do not disclose（不公开）in detail — means that users often do not know why they see certain content, what alternatives they are not seeing, or how their behaviour is being shaped by algorithmic decisions they cannot inspect or challenge.

The concentration of digital platform power（数字平台权力集中）in a small number of companies raises concerns about the democratic accountability（民主问责）of systems that increasingly mediate（中介）public discourse, political communication（政治传播）, commercial activity（商业活动）, and social interaction. These platforms make decisions that affect billions of people — what information they see, what products they encounter, what social connections they form — through processes that are largely invisible to users and subject to limited public oversight（有限的公共监督）.

Digital platforms and algorithms therefore represent the mechanism through which online systems connect users with content, services, and each other and how algorithmic decisions shape what users see, what they engage with, and how their behaviour is influenced. The vocabulary of digital platforms — digital platform, algorithm, algorithmic curation, engagement, transparency, accountability, platform power — names the systems through which billions of people access information and the challenges that arise when those systems operate without transparency or democratic oversight. Media texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from platform design through algorithmic curation to the social outcomes that determine whether digital platforms serve public discourse or undermine it through opaque, engagement-optimised content selection.

## Social Media and Group Identity（社交媒体与群体身份）

Social media（社交媒体）allow users to create and share content, participate in social networking（社交网络）, and form communities（社区）around shared interests, identities, or causes. They have transformed how people communicate, form relationships（建立关系）, express identity（表达身份）, and participate in collective action（参与集体行动）. Social media allow people to connect with others who share their interests, values, or experiences regardless of geographic distance（地理距离）, creating communities that would be impossible in purely physical social environments.

Group identity（群体身份）refers to the part of a person's sense of self（自我意识）that derives from belonging to particular social groups（特定社会群体）— based on nationality（国籍）, ethnicity（民族）, religion（宗教）, profession（职业）, political affiliation（政治归属）, gender（性别）, sexual orientation（性取向）, or shared interests（共同兴趣）. Group identity provides a sense of belonging（归属感）, shared meaning（共同意义）, and social support（社会支持）. It shapes how people perceive the world（感知世界）, evaluate information（评价信息）, and relate to those inside and outside their groups.

Social media can strengthen group identity（强化群体身份）by providing dedicated spaces（专门空间）where group members communicate, share experiences, reinforce shared values, and coordinate action. This strengthening can be positive — support groups（支持群体）for people with rare medical conditions（罕见疾病）, professional networks（职业网络）for knowledge sharing, communities for people with shared cultural backgrounds（共同文化背景）who are geographically dispersed, and activist networks（活动家网络）for social change. These communities provide social support, information, and collective efficacy（集体效能）that members might not find in their immediate physical environment.

Social media can also amplify negative aspects of group identity（放大群体身份的负面方面）. When people interact primarily with others who share their views, opinions can become more extreme through group polarisation（群体极化）— a well-documented psychological process（有充分记录的心理学过程）where group discussion shifts members toward more extreme positions in the direction of the group's initial tendency. Groups can become hostile toward outsiders（对外人敌视）, increasing social division（社会分裂）and reducing the capacity for constructive dialogue across different perspectives. Misinformation（虚假信息）can spread quickly within groups because members trust each other（相互信任）and are less likely to critically evaluate information that confirms shared beliefs.

Algorithms that recommend content similar to what users have already engaged with can create filter bubbles（过滤气泡）— personalised information environments（个性化信息环境）where users are exposed to an increasingly narrow range of perspectives（越来越狭窄的观点范围）. Unlike echo chambers, which result from users' own choices to associate with like-minded people（与志同道合的人交往）, filter bubbles are created by algorithmic systems（算法系统）that users may not be aware of and cannot easily control. The result is that different people can inhabit fundamentally different information environments（根本不同的信息环境）, seeing different facts, different narratives, and different interpretations of the same events, making shared understanding and democratic deliberation increasingly difficult.

Social media and group identity therefore represent the mechanism through which online platforms connect people around shared identities and how those connections can strengthen community bonds while also amplifying polarisation and misinformation. The vocabulary of social media — social media, group identity, group polarisation, filter bubble, echo chamber, collective efficacy — names the platforms through which people connect around shared identities and the psychological processes that determine whether those connections produce positive community outcomes or negative polarisation. Media texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from social media design through group interaction to the identity outcomes that determine whether online communities strengthen social bonds or reinforce division and misinformation.

## Design, Function, and Human Experience（设计、功能与人的体验）

Design（设计）is the intentional process（有意识的过程）of creating objects（物体）, systems（系统）, environments（环境）, communications（传播）, or experiences（体验）that serve specific purposes（特定目的）for specific users. Good design considers not only what something does (its function / 功能) but also how people interact with it（人们如何与之互动）, how it makes them feel（它让他们感觉如何）, and how it fits into the broader context of their lives（它如何融入他们生活的更广泛语境）. Design is present in every human-made object — from the shape of a chair（椅子的形状）to the layout of a website（网站的布局）to the organisation of a city（城市的组织）.

Function（功能）refers to what a designed object or system does — the practical tasks（实际任务）it performs and the problems it solves. A chair supports a person sitting（支撑人坐下）. A website provides information or enables transactions（提供信息或促成交易）. A public transport system moves people between locations（在地点之间运送人员）. A hospital provides medical care（提供医疗服务）. The function of a design determines its basic requirements（基本要求）— a chair must support weight（承受重量）, a website must load quickly（快速加载）, a transport system must be reliable（可靠）. Function is necessary but not sufficient for good design — an object that performs its function but is difficult to use, uncomfortable, ugly, or environmentally harmful（环境有害的）fails to meet the broader goals of design.

Human experience（人的体验）refers to how people feel, think, and respond when they interact with a designed object, system, or environment. Good design considers the user's needs（用户需求）, abilities（能力）, preferences（偏好）, emotions（情感）, and context of use（使用语境）. A well-designed product is not only functional but also intuitive（直观的）— easy to understand and use without extensive instruction; aesthetically pleasing（美观的）— creating positive emotional responses; accessible（可及的）— usable by people with diverse abilities and backgrounds; and sustainable（可持续的）— minimising environmental impact throughout its lifecycle（整个生命周期）.

User-centred design（以用户为中心的设计）places the needs, preferences, and experiences of users at the centre of the design process. Designers research how users will interact with a product（研究用户将如何与产品互动）through observation（观察）, interviews（访谈）, surveys（调查）, and usability testing（可用性测试）. They create prototypes（原型）— preliminary versions（初步版本）of the design — and test them with real users to identify problems, gather feedback, and iterate（迭代）toward improved versions. This iterative process（迭代过程）— design, test, learn, redesign — continues until the product meets users' needs effectively. User-centred design recognises that designers are not their users（设计师不是他们的用户）and that assumptions about what users want or need must be tested against actual user behaviour and feedback.

Design affects every aspect of modern life in ways that are often invisible precisely because good design disappears into the background of daily experience（好的设计融入日常体验的背景中）. The design of a smartphone（智能手机的设计）determines how easily calls, messages, and information are accessed. The design of a building（建筑的设计）affects how people move through it, how they feel inside it, how much energy it consumes（消耗多少能源）, and how it relates to its surroundings（与周围环境的关系）. The design of a public space（公共空间的设计）affects whether people use it, how they interact within it, and whether it creates a sense of community（社区感）or alienation（疏离感）. Design is therefore not merely an aesthetic concern（美学问题）but a social, economic, and environmental one（社会、经济和环境问题）that shapes how people live, work, and relate to each other and the world.

Design, function, and human experience therefore represent the mechanism through which objects, systems, and environments are created to serve specific purposes and how the quality of design determines whether those objects and systems meet human needs effectively and pleasurably. The vocabulary of design — design, function, human experience, user-centred design, prototype, iterative process — names the processes through which designed objects and systems are created and the criteria by which their quality is judged. Media and design texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from design intention through user interaction to the experiential outcomes that determine whether designed objects and systems serve human needs effectively or create frustration and alienation.

## Artistic Expression and Cultural Meaning（艺术表达与文化意义）

Artistic expression（艺术表达）is the use of creative skills（创造性技能）and imagination（想象力）to communicate ideas（传达思想）, emotions（情感）, experiences（体验）, or perspectives（视角）through sensory media（感官媒介）— visual（视觉的）, auditory（听觉的）, kinaesthetic（动觉的）, or linguistic（语言的）. Art takes many forms: painting（绘画）, sculpture（雕塑）, music（音乐）, dance（舞蹈）, theatre（戏剧）, literature（文学）, film（电影）, photography（摄影）, architecture（建筑）, and digital art（数字艺术）. Art can be created for personal expression（个人表达）, communication（交流）, entertainment（娱乐）, social commentary（社会评论）, spiritual practice（精神实践）, political protest（政治抗议）, or aesthetic pleasure（审美愉悦）— often serving multiple purposes simultaneously.

Cultural meaning（文化意义）refers to the significance（意义）that objects, practices, symbols（符号）, and expressions have within a particular cultural context（特定文化语境）. Meaning is not inherent in objects themselves（意义不是物体本身固有的）but is constructed through shared interpretation（共享解释）within cultural communities（文化社群）. A painting may carry different meanings for different viewers depending on their cultural background（文化背景）, personal experience, art historical knowledge（艺术史知识）, and the context in which they encounter it. A national flag（国旗）carries profound meaning for citizens of that nation（对国家公民具有深远意义）but may mean little to outsiders. Cultural meaning changes over time（随时间变化）and varies between groups（因群体而异）as societies evolve, new interpretations emerge, and cultural contexts shift.

Art both reflects and shapes culture（艺术既反映又塑造文化）. Art reflects the values（价值观）, beliefs（信仰）, anxieties（焦虑）, aspirations（抱负）, and social conditions（社会条件）of the society and time in which it is created. A novel written during wartime（战时写的小说）may reflect the anxieties, losses, and moral questions（道德问题）of that period. A painting from the Renaissance（文艺复兴时期的绘画）reflects the humanist values（人文主义价值观）, religious beliefs, and artistic techniques of its era. Art also shapes culture by introducing new ideas（引入新思想）, challenging existing norms（挑战现有规范）, imagining alternative possibilities（想象替代可能性）, and inspiring social change（激发社会变革）. Protest songs（抗议歌曲）, political cartoons（政治漫画）, documentary films（纪录片）, and socially engaged art（社会参与性艺术）can raise awareness（提高意识）, mobilise public opinion（动员舆论）, and contribute to movements for social justice（社会正义运动）.

Different societies have developed distinct traditions of artistic expression（独特的艺术表达传统）shaped by their histories, environments, belief systems, and social structures. Western classical music（西方古典音乐）, Chinese calligraphy（中国书法）and landscape painting（山水画）, Indian classical dance（印度古典舞蹈）, Japanese Noh theatre（日本能剧）, West African drumming（西非鼓乐）, and Aboriginal Australian dot painting（澳大利亚原住民点画）each developed within specific cultural contexts that shaped their forms, purposes, techniques, and aesthetic principles（美学原则）. Understanding these traditions requires understanding the cultural values（文化价值观）, historical contexts（历史语境）, philosophical frameworks（哲学框架）, and social functions（社会功能）that shaped them — art cannot be fully appreciated in isolation from the culture that produced it.

Artistic expression and cultural meaning therefore represent the mechanism through which creative skills and imagination are used to communicate ideas, emotions, and experiences and how those expressions acquire meaning within specific cultural contexts. The vocabulary of art — artistic expression, cultural meaning, cultural context, aesthetic principle, social commentary, socially engaged art — names the forms through which art communicates and the cultural frameworks that determine how art is interpreted and valued. Media and cultural texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from creative expression through cultural interpretation to the meaning outcomes that determine whether art reflects, challenges, or transforms the values and beliefs of the societies in which it is created.

## Cultural Trends and Social Norms（文化趋势与社会规范）

Cultural trends（文化趋势）are patterns of change（变化模式）in the beliefs（信仰）, behaviours（行为）, tastes（品味）, practices（实践）, and expressions of a society over time. Trends can emerge in fashion（时尚）, music, food, language（语言）, technology use, social practices, and values. Some trends are short-lived fads（短暂的时尚）that appear and disappear quickly without lasting impact. Others represent deeper, more lasting changes（更深层、更持久的变化）in how people live, think, and relate to each other — changes in attitudes toward gender roles（性别角色态度）, family structure（家庭结构）, work-life balance（工作与生活平衡）, environmental responsibility（环境责任）, or individual rights（个人权利）.

Social norms（社会规范）are the unwritten rules（不成文规则）— shared expectations（共同期望）and standards（标准）— that govern behaviour in a society or group. Norms shape how people dress（穿着）, speak（说话）, eat（饮食）, work（工作）, interact with others（与他人互动）, and conduct themselves in public（在公共场合的行为）. Norms vary between cultures（因文化而异）and change over time（随时间变化）— what was considered normal and acceptable behaviour fifty years ago may be unacceptable today, and what is normal in one culture may be unusual or offensive in another. Norms are enforced through social approval（社会认可）for conformity（遵从）and social sanctions（社会制裁）— disapproval（不赞成）, exclusion（排斥）, ridicule（嘲笑）— for violation（违反）.

Cultural trends and social norms influence each other in a dynamic relationship（动态关系）. A cultural trend can challenge existing norms and eventually change them. Jeans（牛仔裤）began as casual workwear（休闲工作服）and eventually changed norms about what clothing is appropriate in professional and formal settings（专业和正式场合）. Sharing personal information on social media has changed norms about privacy（隐私规范）, with younger generations generally accepting greater public disclosure（公共披露）than older generations. Remote work（远程工作）has changed norms about workplace presence（工作场所出勤）, professional communication（职业沟通）, and the boundary between work and personal life.

Globalisation（全球化）has accelerated the flow of cultural trends across national borders（加速文化趋势跨国流动）. Fashion trends from Paris（巴黎）and Milan（米兰）spread globally within weeks. Korean pop music（韩国流行音乐 / K-pop）has fans across every continent. American films and television shows are consumed worldwide. Japanese animation（日本动画 / anime）has a global audience. Chinese social media platforms（中国社交媒体平台）and digital trends influence users internationally. This cultural exchange（文化交流）can enrich societies by exposing people to different ways of living, thinking, creating, and expressing themselves — broadening perspectives（拓宽视野）and fostering cross-cultural understanding（促进跨文化理解）.

Global cultural flows（全球文化流动）can also threaten local cultural traditions（威胁当地文化传统）when dominant global media and cultural products（主导性全球媒体和文化产品）displace local languages（取代当地语言）, music（音乐）, storytelling traditions（讲故事传统）, and cultural practices. The tension between global cultural integration（全球文化融合）and local cultural preservation（当地文化保护）is an important issue in many societies, raising questions about cultural sovereignty（文化主权）, cultural diversity（文化多样性）, and the value of maintaining distinct cultural identities（维护独特文化身份的价值）in an increasingly interconnected world.

Cultural trends and social norms therefore represent the mechanism through which beliefs, behaviours, and practices change over time and how those changes are shaped by the interaction between cultural innovation and social enforcement. The vocabulary of culture — cultural trend, social norm, fad, cultural exchange, global cultural flow, cultural sovereignty — names the patterns through which culture changes and the forces that determine whether those changes enrich or threaten local cultural traditions. Media and cultural texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from cultural innovation through social adoption to the norm outcomes that determine whether societies become more diverse and open or whether global cultural flows displace local traditions and reduce cultural diversity.

## Identity, Representation, and Social Change（身份、再现与社会变化）

Identity（身份）refers to a person's sense of who they are（自我认知）— shaped by personal characteristics（个人特征）, life experiences（生活经历）, social group memberships（社会群体成员身份）, cultural background, and the interactions between these elements. Identity is not fixed（不固定的）but dynamic（动态的）— it can change over time, vary across different contexts（在不同语境中变化）, and encompass multiple dimensions（包含多个维度）simultaneously. A person may identify as a parent（父母）, a professional（专业人士）, a member of an ethnic community（民族社区成员）, a citizen of a country（国家公民）, and a participant in a global online community（全球在线社区参与者）, with different aspects of identity becoming more or less salient（显著）depending on the situation.

Representation（再现 / 表征）refers to how people, groups, ideas, and experiences are portrayed（描绘）in media, art, literature, advertising（广告）, political discourse（政治话语）, and other cultural products. Representation is not a neutral reflection of reality（不是现实的中立反映）but a constructed portrayal（建构的描绘）that involves choices about what to include（包含什么）, what to exclude（排除什么）, how to characterise（如何刻画）, and what narratives（什么叙事）to use. Representation shapes how people see themselves（人们如何看待自己）and how they are seen by others（他人如何看待他们）. When certain groups are consistently underrepresented（持续代表性不足）, misrepresented（被错误呈现）, or represented through stereotypes（通过刻板印象呈现）, it can reinforce social inequality（强化社会不平等）, limit aspirations（限制抱负）, and perpetuate discrimination（延续歧视）.

Movements for more diverse and accurate representation（更多元化和准确再现的运动）have called for media, art, advertising, and other cultural products to reflect the actual diversity of human experience — including people of different races（不同种族）, ethnicities（民族）, genders（性别）, sexual orientations（性取向）, abilities（能力）, ages（年龄）, body types（体型）, and socioeconomic backgrounds（社会经济背景）. The goal is for cultural products to represent the world as it actually is（按照世界的真实面貌呈现世界）— diverse, complex, and multifaceted（多面的）— rather than through a narrow lens（狭隘的视角）that centres the experiences and perspectives of dominant groups.

Social change（社会变化）refers to significant transformations（重大转变）in the structure, institutions（制度）, values, and practices of a society over time. Social change can be driven by technological innovation（技术创新）, economic development（经济发展）, political movements（政治运动）, cultural shifts（文化转变）, demographic changes（人口变化）, environmental pressures（环境压力）, and the interactions among these forces. Media and culture play important roles in social change by shaping how people understand social issues（人们如何理解社会问题）, what they consider possible or desirable（认为什么是可能的或可取的）, and what they are willing to act to achieve.

Media can support social change by raising awareness of injustices（提高对不公正的认识）, giving voice to marginalised groups（为边缘化群体发声）, mobilising public support（动员公众支持）for reform, and holding powerful institutions accountable（追究强权机构的责任）. Investigative journalism（调查新闻）has exposed corruption（腐败）, environmental destruction, and human rights abuses（人权侵犯）. Social media has enabled grassroots movements（草根运动）to organise, communicate, and mobilise at unprecedented scale and speed. Documentary films（纪录片）and literature have changed public understanding of issues from poverty to mental health to climate change. Media can also resist social change（抵制社会变化）by reinforcing existing power structures（强化现有权力结构）, promoting dominant narratives（推广主导叙事）that marginalise alternative perspectives, and creating distraction（制造分心）from issues that require public attention and action.

Identity, representation, and social change therefore represent the mechanism through which people understand themselves and others through cultural representation and how media and culture shape the possibilities for social transformation. The vocabulary of identity and representation — identity, representation, stereotype, social change, grassroots movement, investigative journalism — names the processes through which identity is formed and expressed and the cultural forces that either support or resist social change. Media and cultural texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from identity formation through cultural representation to the social change outcomes that determine whether media and culture reinforce existing power structures or challenge them in ways that create more just and inclusive societies.
